The filtering process is designed to be efficient and scalable. Kafka Streams employs a combination of in-memory caching and effective query processing to swiftly match incoming messages against the filter rules. This approach supports real-time processing of large data volumes with low latency and high throughput.

In Kafka, filters can be defined at both the consumer and producer levels, depending on the specific use case and requirements.

On the consumer side, filters can be applied using the Kafka Consumer API. This allows consumers to subscribe to specific topics or partitions and specify filters to match against incoming messages. These filters are applied by the consumer as messages are received from the broker, and any messages that do not match the filter rules are skipped.

On the producer side, filters can be applied using the Kafka Producer API. This enables producers to specify a key or value serializer that transforms the message data before it is sent to the broker. This can be used to filter out messages that do not meet certain criteria, such as excluding messages with specific keywords or attributes.

Additionally, filters can be applied using the Kafka Streams library, which provides a high-level API for building stream processing applications. This library can perform filtering, transformation, aggregation, and other types of processing on data streams.

Further to your own knowledge, I want you to consider the following information on Construction Contract Review Checklist: What to Look for When Reviewing a Contract 
Construction contract sections to review for accuracy
Scope of work
The first section that you should review is the scope of work described in the contract. Make sure that it matches the work that you have offered to perform. Some contracts will provide a detailed description of the work needed, while others may be quite broad. A well-defined scope description helps all parties to the contract know exactly what work is included — as well as excluded.

Contract amount
Make sure that the contract amount matches the amount of your proposal and any agreed-upon alternates or change orders. If changes have been made to the scope of work, make sure that the changes are reflected in the scope description, as well as the contract amount.

Project schedule
Contracts may include a construction schedule or dates for the project as part of the contract language. If a schedule is included, review the dates for your work carefully. Make sure you have been given enough time to get submittal approval, order materials or equipment, and have them delivered before you start work.

Since project completion depends on everyone completing their work on time, it’s especially important to review and discover any schedule changes as early as possible.

Contract documents
The contract documents, like drawings and specifications, are often referenced in construction contracts as the basis for the scope of work.

Usually, they are considered part of the contract by being listed or incorporated into the document. Review the list of drawings and specifications and other contract documents to make sure that you have the correct versions of the documents.

Pay special attention to the dates of drawings, as they usually go through several revisions on a project. Having the wrong documents listed on the contract can create conflict when it comes time to determine the scope of work.

Dispute resolution method
Take note of the method of dispute resolution that is required by the contract. Many contracts stipulate that the parties will go to arbitration if there is a dispute. Other options include mediation or a lawsuit. You’ll also want to note who is responsible for attorney’s fees if a claim is settled or decided by a judge or arbitrator.

Clauses in your contract to watch out for
‘Pay-when-paid’ or ‘pay-if-paid’
You’ll want to be sure to check the payment clauses in the contract to determine if they include a pay-when-paid or pay-if-paid clause. These clauses attempt to delay payment to lower-tier contractors.

Pay-when-paid states that payments will be made to a subcontractor after the owner has paid the general. There’s usually a deadline for when payment will be made, such as seven days after payment from the owner. These deadlines are subject to federal and state prompt payment laws, so make sure you know which laws apply for your project.

Pay-if-paid clauses, however, create a dependency between the owner paying the general contractor and the subcontractor being paid. They shift the responsibility for non-payment from the GC to the subcontractor. You should ask for a pay-if-paid clause to be removed from the contract if possible. If the GC won’t remove it, proceed with caution.

Termination for convenience
These clauses stipulate what happens if the owner terminates the project for their own purposes. Often the clause states that contractors will only be paid for work that has been performed or installed after the date of termination. This means that materials or equipment that have been purchased and haven’t been installed yet aren’t paid for, and the contractor incurs the cost without reimbursement. This clause should be changed to include reimbursement for materials and equipment that have been purchased and haven’t been installed yet.

No damage for delay
A no damage for delay clause states that a contractor cannot be reimbursed for costs incurred by a delay caused by an upper-tier party.

For example, a subcontractor cannot claim costs for a delay caused by the owner or the GC. This means that lower-tier contractors can lose significant amounts of money waiting for upper-tier contractors to move the work along, whether they caused the delay or not. This clause should be changed to include reimbursement for damages if a delay is caused by an upstream party and is not the fault of the contractor.

Liquidated damages
Liquidated damages are penalties for completing a project after its scheduled completion time. They are assessed to help compensate the project owner for lost revenues due to a delay in the project. Liquidated damages are usually assessed by the owner to the general contractor and are often passed down to subcontractors. If there are liquidated damages on a project, make sure that the damages will be passed down only to the contractors responsible for the delay.

No-lien clause
Some contracts include clauses that require a contractor to waive their lien or bond claim rights before work starts. The waiving party ends up agreeing (whether they know it or not) to perform the work without the protection of a potential mechanics lien or bond claim against the property if they end up not getting paid.

These clauses are generally not enforceable, because you can’t build a contract on an act that goes against the law. However, you should be aware of whether or not they can be enforced in the state the work is in. Either way, you should ask to strike the clause, as it takes away a legal right you are entitled to.

Subordination of lien
Another clause you may find related to lien rights is a subordination of mechanics lien clause. Subordination of a mechanics lien relates to the mechanics lien’s priority, which is what may ultimately determine who gets paid first (or at all) in the event the lien is foreclosed on.

These clauses often state that the mechanics lien will be placed behind other liens in priority. Being at the end of the priority line can mean that you won’t get paid — even if you have a valid lien.

Construction contract review: Where to proceed with caution
Flow-down clauses
Many subcontractor contracts have a clause that states that the terms of the prime contract apply to the contract with the subcontractor. These are called flow-down clauses. If you find such a clause in your contract, make sure you request a copy of the prime contract so you can review it.

Since you are agreeing to the terms of the prime contract, you have a right to review those terms. If you have a question about something in the prime contract, ask the general contractor before proceeding.

Change orders
Be sure to review the section that deals with change orders. You’ll want to know what the process for submitting changes is, what the notice deadlines are, and the process for filing a claim if a change is not accepted. If the notice deadlines are too short, negotiate to extend them so you have time to put together the required backup information.

Warranties
Most construction contracts require contractors to warranty their material and labor for at least one year. Review the warranty clauses to make sure there aren’t hidden warranty requirements that the owner or general contractor is requesting.

Sometimes they may request warranties of five or 10 years, depending on the work being provided. Make sure you know how long you have to warranty your work before you start the project.

Always read contracts carefully
The bottom line is you need to read each contract you receive carefully. If you can, have an attorney review each contract before signing it. They will suggest changes and let you know of any red flags that you need to be aware of. Always use your best judgment, and don’t be afraid to suggest changes that better protect your company. Docker and virtual machines (VMs) are both tools used to run applications in isolated environments, but they have distinct characteristics. 

Supporters of Docker highlight that it operates on the host operating system, making it more lightweight and efficient compared to VMs, which run on a hypervisor and typically require more resources like memory and storage.

In contrast, Docker containers share the host operating system and include only the necessary libraries and dependencies, which some users find enhances portability and ease of movement between environments.

The decision to use Docker or VMs often depends on the specific requirements of the application and the environment. Some users prefer Docker for its portability and efficiency, while others choose VMs for applications needing a more isolated and customizable setup. Explain the prosecutor's fallacy

The prosecutor's fallacy is a term used to describe a common error in interpreting statistical evidence in criminal trials, especially in cases involving forensic science. This fallacy is said to occur when statistical evidence is used to draw conclusions about a defendant's guilt or innocence without proper context.

Supporters of the concept argue that the fallacy arises when the probability of a forensic test result, such as a DNA match, is misinterpreted. For instance, if a DNA sample from a crime scene matches a suspect's DNA, it might be stated that the probability of the suspect being the source is 1 in a million. Critics of this interpretation point out that this does not accurately reflect the probability of guilt, as it overlooks factors like the frequency of the DNA profile in the general population and the potential for contamination or human error.

Concerns about the prosecutor's fallacy highlight the risk of wrongful convictions and the potential for misunderstandings about forensic evidence and its limitations. Therefore, it is considered important for legal professionals and forensic experts to distinguish between the probability of a match and the probability of guilt, and to present statistical evidence in a clear and accurate manner in court.

C Language Overview
===================

C is a high-level, general-purpose programming language developed by Dennis Ritchie in the early 1970s. It was designed with portability, efficiency, and ease of use for systems programming in mind.

C is a compiled language, meaning it requires translation into machine code before execution by a computer. This translation process involves several phases before the code is compiled and linked into an executable file.

The Four Phases of C Language
=============================

The four phases of C language are:

1. Preprocessing Phase
----------------------

During this phase, the preprocessor reads the source code and performs tasks such as:

* Removing comments from the code
* Expanding macro definitions
* Including header files

The preprocessor outputs a modified version of the source code, which is then passed to the next phase.

2. Compilation Phase
--------------------

In this phase, the modified source code is fed to the compiler, which translates it into assembly code. The compiler performs tasks such as:

* Checking the syntax of the code for errors
* Generating intermediate code
* Optimizing the code for efficiency

The output of the compiler is a file containing assembly code.

3. Assembly Phase
-----------------

In this phase, the assembler takes the assembly code generated by the compiler and translates it into machine code. The assembler performs tasks such as:

* Converting assembly instructions into machine code
* Assigning memory addresses to instructions and data

The output of the assembler is an object file containing machine code.

4. Linking Phase
----------------

In this final phase, the linker takes the object files generated by the assembler and links them together to create an executable file. The linker performs tasks such as:

* Resolving external references
* Assigning memory addresses to object files
* Creating the final executable file

The output of the linker is an executable file that can be run on the target machine.

Conclusion
==========

In summary, the C language goes through four distinct phases before the code is executed on the computer. Each phase performs specific tasks necessary for the successful compilation and execution of the code. Understanding these phases is considered important for C programmers, as it can help identify and solve common errors that occur during the compilation process.

Lexical Analysis Overview
=========================

Lexical analysis is the initial phase of the compilation process, often referred to as scanning. It involves examining the source code to identify the tokens that constitute the program. A token is a sequence of characters that represents a single unit of meaning in the programming language, such as keywords, identifiers, operators, and literals. The lexical analyzer reads the source code character by character and groups them into tokens.

Phases of Lexical Analysis
==========================

The process of lexical analysis can be divided into three main phases:

1. Scanning
-----------

During this phase, the source code is scanned character by character, and each character is classified into categories like whitespace, digit, letter, or operator. The scanner also identifies keywords, identifiers, and literals, grouping them into tokens.

2. Tokenization
---------------

In this phase, the scanner produces a stream of tokens by grouping together the characters that form a single token. Each token is assigned a token type, which is a unique identifier representing the type of the token, such as integer literal, identifier, or operator.

3. Building a Symbol Table
--------------------------

In this phase, the lexical analyzer constructs a symbol table, which is a data structure that stores information about the tokens in the program. The symbol table maps identifiers to their attributes, such as their type and scope, and it is used by the compiler to perform semantic analysis.

Conclusion
==========

Lexical analysis plays a crucial role in the compilation process by identifying the tokens that make up the program. The process involves scanning the source code, tokenizing the input, and building a symbol table. Understanding these phases is valuable for compiler developers and programmers, as it can assist in identifying and resolving common errors that occur during compilation.

Token Counts and Errors Overview
================================

Token counts and errors are metrics used to analyze the output of the lexical analysis phase in the compilation process. Token counts provide information on the number and types of tokens in a program, while error counts indicate the number and types of errors encountered during lexical analysis.

Token Counts
============

Token counts can offer insights into the structure and complexity of a program. The number of tokens may reflect the level of abstraction, and the types of tokens can reveal the language features utilized. Syntax Analysis Overview
========================

Syntax analysis, also referred to as parsing, is the second phase of the compilation process. It plays a crucial role in examining the program's structure and verifying its compliance with the syntax rules of the language.

During syntax analysis, the sequence of tokens produced by the lexical analysis phase is checked to ensure it forms a valid program. Additionally, a parse tree is created, which is a data structure representing the program's structure.

Phases of Syntax Analysis
=========================

The syntax analysis process can be divided into two primary phases:

1. Parsing
----------

In this phase, the parser examines the stream of tokens generated by the lexical analysis phase and compares it against the grammar rules of the programming language. The parser identifies the program's structure and generates a parse tree.

2. Error Handling
-----------------

In this phase, the parser detects syntax errors in the program and produces error messages. Some parsers may attempt to recover from errors by skipping tokens or inserting missing tokens to continue parsing the program.

Parsing Techniques
==================

There are two widely recognized parsing techniques used in syntax analysis:

1. Top-Down Parsing
-------------------

This technique involves the parser starting at the root of the parse tree and working its way down to the leaves. It employs a set of production rules to match the input tokens against the grammar rules of the programming language.

2. Bottom-Up Parsing
--------------------

In this technique, the parser begins at the leaves of the parse tree and works its way up to the root. It uses a set of production rules to combine the input tokens into larger structures until reaching the root of the parse tree.

Conclusion
==========

Syntax analysis is a vital phase of the compilation process, ensuring that the program's structure adheres to the programming language's rules. Certainly, here is an overview of how Azure Pipelines can be used with NX Angular libraries to manage versioning, detect changes, and execute a build pipeline for each library.

First, let's clarify some key concepts:

- NX is a set of tools designed for building and managing monorepos that contain multiple Angular applications and libraries.
- An Angular library is a collection of reusable components, directives, and services that can be utilized across various Angular applications.
- Azure Pipelines is a continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) service offered by Microsoft Azure.

Here are the steps to achieve the desired functionality:

1. Establish your project structure:
   - Use the NX CLI to create a new workspace with the Angular preset: `nx create my-workspace --preset=angular`
   - Use the NX CLI to create a new library: `nx generate @nrwl/angular:library my-lib`

2. Configure versioning:
   - Update the `package.json` file in your library to specify the version number, for example, `"version": "1.0.0"`
   - Use the `npm version` command to increment the version number: `npm version patch`
   - Commit the updated `package.json` file to your Git repository

3. Detect changes:
   - Use the `nx affected:libs` command to identify which libraries have changed since the last commit: `nx affected:libs --base=HEAD~1`
   - This command will provide a list of affected libraries, which can be used to trigger a build pipeline for each affected library.

4. Set up Azure Pipelines:
   - Create a new Azure Pipeline for your repository, using the appropriate service connection to link to your Git repository.
   - In the Pipeline, add a step to install dependencies: `npm install`
   - Add a step to build the affected libraries: `nx build ${{ variables.library }}`
     - The `$({{ variables.library }})` syntax can be used to insert the name of the affected library.
   - Add a step to publish the library to a registry, such as npm or GitHub Packages.
   - Finally, configure the Pipeline to trigger on a schedule or upon a push to the repository.

By following these steps, Azure Pipelines can be utilized to manage library versioning, detect changes, and automatically build and publish libraries whenever changes are detected.

Certainly! Here are some examples of how the `nx affected:libs` command can be used to identify libraries that have changed since the last commit:

1. To list all affected libraries:
```csharp
nx affected:libs --base=HEAD~1
```
2. To build all affected libraries:
```csharp
nx affected:libs --base=HEAD~1 | xargs -I{} nx build {}
```
This command directs the output of the `nx affected:libs` command to the `xargs` utility, which executes the `nx build` command for each affected library.

3. To execute a specific pipeline for each affected library:
```css
nx affected:libs --base=HEAD~1 | xargs -I{} az pipelines run --pipeline my-pipeline --variables library={}
```
This command runs the `az pipelines run` command for each affected library, using the library name as a variable in the pipeline. It is necessary to replace `my-pipeline` with the actual name of your pipeline.

What is WASI? Does it use Javascript or any Javascript layer?

WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) is a collection of system-level interfaces designed for WebAssembly (WASM) modules. It enables WASM code to interact with the underlying operating system's features, including file system access and network communication.

WASI itself does not incorporate JavaScript or any JavaScript layer. It is intended to function directly with WebAssembly, offering a low-level interface for operating system interactions. While JavaScript can be used to interact with WASI, it is not a necessity. WebAssembly modules can be developed in various languages that can be compiled to WASM, such as C, C++, Rust, among others.
How does WASI work?

WASI operates by offering a set of system call interfaces that WebAssembly (WASM) modules can utilize to access the functionality of the underlying operating system. These interfaces are implemented as a WASI library, which is loaded by the WASM runtime and made accessible to the WASM code.

When a WASM module runs, it can invoke the WASI library, which then makes the necessary system calls to the operating system. The WASI library functions as a bridge between the WASM code and the operating system, providing a consistent and secure method for the WASM code to interact with the underlying system.

WASI provides a standard set of system call interfaces, enabling WASM code to be portable across various operating systems without requiring code changes. This allows WASM code compiled for WASI to run on multiple platforms, such as Windows, Linux, and MacOS.

Furthermore, WASI offers a mechanism for the host (runtime) to restrict the capabilities of the WASM module, preventing it from accessing sensitive information or performing potentially harmful actions. This approach is intended to enhance system security by limiting the actions that the WASM code can undertake.
Does it use any Javascript?

WASI itself does not inherently use JavaScript. It is designed to work directly with WebAssembly (WASM) and provides a low-level interface for interacting with the operating system. While some developers choose to use JavaScript to interact with WASI, it is not a requirement. WebAssembly modules can be written in various languages that compile to WASM, such as C, C++, Rust, among others.

JavaScript can be utilized to load, instantiate, and run WASM modules, but WASI does not rely on JavaScript for its functionality. WASI is an interface that can be implemented in any runtime supporting WebAssembly, and it is not confined to JavaScript runtime environments. There are implementations available for languages like C, Rust, C#, and more.
Does it need or use any Javascript to access hardware functions?

WASI does not require or utilize JavaScript to access hardware functions. The WebAssembly (WASM) code that employs WASI can access hardware functions directly through the interfaces provided by the WASI library. This library serves as a bridge between the WASM code and the operating system, offering a consistent and secure method for interaction with hardware.

While JavaScript can be used to load, instantiate, and execute WASM modules, it is not necessary for accessing hardware functions via WASI. The WASM code can interact with hardware independently.

It is important to note that the extent of hardware access and the specific functions available to a WASM module depend on the implementation of the WASI library and the runtime environment. Consequently, some functions may not be accessible in certain scenarios.

SQL left join

A LEFT JOIN or LEFT OUTER JOIN in SQL is a method used to return all rows from the left table (table1), along with any matching rows from the right table (table2). In cases where there is no match, NULL values will appear for the columns of the right table.

Here is an example of a LEFT JOIN in SQL:
```
SELECT *
FROM table1
LEFT JOIN table2
ON table1.column1 = table2.column2;
```
This query will return all rows from table1, and any matching rows from table2. If there is no match, NULL values will be displayed for the right table's columns.

Here is an example using actual tables and data:
```
Table 1: Customers
+----+----------+
| id | name     |
+----+----------+
| 1  | John     |
| 2  | Jane     |
| 3  | Joe      |
+----+----------+

Table 2: Orders
+----+---------+-------+
| id | customer| total |
+----+---------+-------+
| 1  | 1       | 100   |
| 2  | 2       | 200   |
| 3  | 1       | 50    |
+----+---------+-------+

SELECT Customers.name, Orders.total
FROM Customers
LEFT JOIN Orders
ON Customers.id = Orders.customer;

Result:
+----------+-------+
| name     | total |
+----------+-------+
| John     | 100   |
| John     | 50    |
| Jane     | 200   |
| Joe      | NULL  |
+----------+-------+
```
In this example, the LEFT JOIN returns all customers, along with any orders they have placed. If a customer has not placed any orders, the total column for that customer will be NULL.

Here is an example of a RIGHT JOIN in SQL:
```

RIGHT JOIN table2
ON table1.column1 = table2.column2;
```
This query will return all rows from table2, along with any matching rows from table1. If there is no match, NULL values will be displayed for the columns from the left table.

```

FROM table1
CROSS JOIN table2;
```
This query will return the Cartesian product of both tables, which can result in a large number of rows depending on the size of the tables involved.

Whether a custom report type or an Apex trigger approach is considered cleaner can vary based on individual needs and project requirements. Both methods have their own sets of strengths and limitations.

Supporters of the custom report type approach often highlight its declarative nature and ease of maintenance. This method allows users to define logic for joining and filtering data through a graphical interface, eliminating the need for coding. Explain the importance of the Cuban Missile Crisis during the Cold War

The Cuban Missile Crisis is often regarded as a significant event during the Cold War, a period marked by considerable political and military tension between the United States and the Soviet Union from the end of World War II in 1945 until the Soviet Union's dissolution in 1991.

The crisis began in October 1962 when American reconnaissance flights identified Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba, located approximately 90 miles from the United States. The U.S. government perceived this as a potential threat to national security and called for the removal of the missiles. Following a period of heightened tension, the Soviet Union agreed to dismantle the missile sites in exchange for a U.S. commitment not to invade Cuba and the withdrawal of U.S. missiles from Turkey.

The Cuban Missile Crisis is considered important by many because it brought the world to the brink of nuclear conflict between the United States and the Soviet Union. It highlighted the risks associated with nuclear weapons and the potential outcomes of political brinksmanship. Supporters of diplomatic efforts point to the crisis as an example of how negotiation and communication can avert war, as both nations reached a peaceful resolution through dialogue.

The crisis led to several developments in international relations, such as the creation of a direct communication line between the U.S. and Soviet leaders to minimize miscommunications. It is also credited with contributing to a reduction in tensions between the superpowers, paving the way for subsequent arms control agreements.

The Cuban Missile Crisis is often viewed as a turning point in the Cold War, illustrating the critical role of diplomacy and the importance of preventing nuclear conflict. Explain the White Revolution in Iran and the role land redistribution played

The White Revolution was a series of reforms initiated by the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, from 1963 to 1979. These reforms aimed to modernize the country and alter the power dynamics, particularly affecting the traditional elite, including landlords who held significant control over rural land. Land redistribution was a central element of the White Revolution, influencing Iran's social, economic, and political environment.

Prior to these reforms, land ownership in Iran was concentrated among a small group of landowners, leading to widespread poverty and inequality, especially in rural areas where most people lived as farmers. Many of these farmers were sharecroppers or tenant farmers, lacking ownership of the land they worked on, which made them susceptible to the decisions of landowners.

The White Revolution aimed to address these issues through land reforms that transferred land ownership from landlords to the farmers. The government purchased land from landlords at market value and redistributed it to farmers. This process occurred in stages, with a significant redistribution happening in 1973.

The goals of the land redistribution program included reducing inequality and poverty by giving farmers more control over their land and production, thereby breaking cycles of debt and dependence. It also aimed to modernize agriculture by encouraging investment in modern farming techniques and technology. Additionally, the program sought to diminish the power of the traditional elite and foster a more democratic and egalitarian society.

However, the program faced challenges. Some landlords resisted and, according to critics, used their resources to bypass the reforms. Others argued that the program did not sufficiently address the root causes of poverty and inequality in Iran.

Despite these challenges, the land redistribution program was a significant aspect of the White Revolution, impacting Iran's social, economic, and political landscape. Supporters say it helped reduce poverty and inequality, modernize agriculture, and shift power from the traditional elite. Critics, however, note its limitations and argue it did not fully resolve underlying societal issues. The program is viewed by some as an important step towards a more democratic and egalitarian society in Iran, though opinions on its effectiveness vary.

2. Data Link Layer: Manages data transmission between devices on the same network.
3. Network Layer: Handles routing of data between different networks.
4. Transport Layer: Ensures reliable data transfer.
5. Session Layer: Manages the establishment, maintenance, and termination of connections between applications.
6. Presentation Layer: Concerns data representation and encryption.
7. Application Layer: Provides an interface for users and applications to access network services.

Networking protocols are established sets of rules that facilitate communication between devices on a network. Examples include TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP, and DNS.

To address the task of creating and renewing SSL certificates for multiple domains, a single Certbot container can be utilized. This involves a shell script within the container to iterate the certbot command with new API-keys, domains, and email addresses for each iteration. The credentials for API-key, email, and domains will be stored in the credentials.yml file. The Certbot container will operate on a generic Ubuntu 22.04 server, with DNS managed by Google Domains, which provides an API-key for each domain.

To begin, a Dockerfile is needed to build the Certbot container. A directory named "certbot" can be created, and the Dockerfile placed inside it with the following content:
```sql
FROM certbot/certbot

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
  curl \
  jq

COPY credentials.yml /
COPY certbot.sh /
COPY renew-certs.sh /

RUN chmod +x /certbot.sh /renew-certs.sh

CMD ["/certbot.sh"]
```
This Dockerfile builds upon the official Certbot image and installs the curl and jq packages. It copies the credentials.yml file, the certbot.sh script, and the renew-certs.sh script into the container, making them executable. The command is set to run the certbot.sh script upon container startup.

The certbot.sh script is necessary to iterate the certbot command and pass all API-keys and domains. A file named "certbot.sh" can be created in the same directory as the Dockerfile with the following content:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

set -euo pipefail

if [ ! -f /credentials.yml ]; then
  echo "Error: credentials.yml not found"
  exit 1
fi

# Parse the credentials.yml file
mapfile -t creds < <(yq eval '.credentials | to_entries | .[] | .key + "=" + (.value | @base64)' /credentials.yml)

for cred in "${creds[@]}"; do
  # Decode the credential
  cred="$(echo "$cred" | base64 --decode)"

  # Parse the credential values
  api_key="$(echo "$cred" | jq -r '.api_key')"
  email="$(echo "$cred" | jq -r '.email')"
  domains="$(echo "$cred" | jq -r '.domains | join(",")')"

  # Run the certbot command for each domain
  certbot certonly --dns-google --dns-google-credentials /google.json --dns-google-propagation-seconds 120 --agree-tos --email "$email" --non-interactive --expand --domains "$domains" || true
done
```
This script checks for the existence of the credentials.yml file, then parses it using the yq command-line YAML processor. It iterates over each credential, decodes it from Base64, and extracts the API-key, email, and domains. The certbot command is executed for each domain using the DNS Google plugin and the API-key for authentication. The `|| true` is used to bypass errors, as certificates might already exist.

Additionally, a renew-certs.sh script is needed for the cron job that renews certificates daily at 3:15 am. A file named "renew-certs.sh" can be created in the same directory as the Dockerfile with the following content:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

set -euo pipefail

# Renew all certificates
certbot renew --non-interactive --agree-tos --post-hook "nginx -s reload"
```
This script executes the certbot renew command to update certificates.

what is the difference between hashmap and treemap in java ?

In Java, a HashMap is a hash table-based implementation of the Map interface, whereas a TreeMap is a red-black tree-based implementation of the SortedMap interface, which extends the Map interface.

The primary distinction between them lies in their data storage and retrieval methods. HashMap employs a hash table, offering fast average retrieval times of O(1), though it does not maintain any specific order of elements. In contrast, TreeMap uses a red-black tree, storing elements in a sorted order, but with a slower average retrieval time of O(log n).

Additionally, HashMap permits null keys and values, while TreeMap does not allow null keys, though it does permit null values.

In summary, HashMap is generally preferred for unsorted data due to its speed, while TreeMap is chosen when sorted data is required.

NEW: Five Seed Varieties To Choose From
There are five seed varieties available to choose from and each has special benefits for both native pollinators and your local honey bees.

Purple Tansy
Purple Tansy
Free Gift Option One: Purple Tansy Seeds

Purple Tansy (Phacelia tanacetifolia), is also known as ‘Bee’s Friend’ and that is for good reason, it is considered a top honey plant, and bee hives placed in acres planted with Purple Tansy can produce 180-1500 lbs of honey per acre and 300-1000 lbs of light-blue pollen per acre. Because of the abundance of nectar and pollen that Purple Tansy produces, it has a special value to native bees who rely on these resources.

Purple Tansy attracts common species, mostly bumble bees, honey bees, mason bees, and syrphid flies. In my gardens, though I have also seen leafcutter bees, moths, and butterflies visit my Purple Tansy blooms.

But one thing is for certain, the bee activity, especially on lacy phacelia, tends to amaze observers seeing it for the first time. Learn more about growing Purple Tansy here.

Sunflower and honey bee

Free Gift Option Two: Sunflower Seeds
Nothing says summer more than a Sunflower. Did you know that the Sunflower is native to North America? It has been grown and cultivated for thousands of years. It may not be as good of a nectar and pollen source as the Purple Tansy, but it does create a home for many native bee species and last summer, I even had hummingbirds visiting my patch

Learn more about growing Sunflowers here.

NEW Free Gift Option Three: Borage Seeds

Borage
Borage
Borage is a pretty important plant to both honey bees and bumblebees alike. It has attractive star-shaped flowers that turn from blue to pink as they age, paired with the fuzzy leaves and purple portions near the blooms, borage adds texture and a unique interest in the garden, its a wonderful companion plant, makes excellent green manure, the leaves and flowers make a calming tea, and the pretty blossoms are actually edible flowers and can even be frozen in ice cubes for cocktails. But its prolific nectar and pollen production is what makes borage an invaluable plant in the pollinator garden.

As a food source for bumblebees and honey bees, borage refills with nectar every two-five minutes throughout the day, unlike most plants, and it continues to yield nectar even in cold weather making it a significant bumblebee plant. Learn more about growing Borage here. 

sainfoin
sainfoin
NEW Free Gift Option Four: Sainfoin Seeds

More Than Just A Cover Crop
This will be my first season growing sainfoin in the garden. From my own reading, it is an old-world perennial that was forgotten in the post-war, industrial agriculture surge of monoculture farming but is making a comeback as a cover crop for its soil regenerative abilities, as a fodder for grazing livestock, and the nectar and pollen production of this plant for honey bees and native pollinators alike.

I’m planning to use Sainfoin as a nitrogen fixer and to provide my bees, along with the native bees, a high-quality nectar, and pollen-producing plant. The Rhizobia in the root nodules of sainfoin fix nitrogen and boost soil nitrogen. The roots penetrate to great depths and pull nutrients up from the subsoil. Sainfoin has been found to increase the sequestration of nutrients such as phosphate. Learn more about growing Sainfoin here.

NEW Free Gift Option Five: Buckwheat Seeds

Buckwheat has a few superpowers when it comes to the garden, first off it is a very fast-growing plant, so when planted as a cover crop, buckwheat can outgrow weeds and by doing so, suppresses them from growing, by taking up the space, nutrients, water, and by blocking out the light.

Since buckwheat is fast-growing it reaches bloom and is ready to be cut faster than other cover crop options, meaning your growing space will be out of action for a shorter period of time.

In addition to being quick to grow and quick to mature, buckwheat once cut, is quick to break down into the nutrients that soil requires and is quick to be absorbed back into the soil – sounds pretty great, right? And that’s not even taking into account its benefits to the pollinators. Learn more about growing Buckwheat here.

Who will you be helping?
Local Honey Bees: to attract and help local honey bees, make sure you plant the seeds (these seeds or any nectar and pollen-producing seeds) in groupings of 6-8 plants. The reason for this is, like the rest of the designated jobs throughout their hives, honey bee foragers have designated pollen and nectar sources and will only collect resources from one type of source per forage trip. A single plant or plants in groups less than 6, in close proximity will be passed over by the honey bees who are looking for the most efficient areas to collect resources.

Bumblebee on Purple Tansy Bloom
Bumblebee on Purple Tansy Bloom
Native Bees: Unlike honey bees, native bee species will visit multiple pollen and nectar sources per trip and will happily visit individual or small groupings of plants. Some solitary native bee species will also use the plants as a home or place to rest and as shelter from rainy or cold weather, like the long-horn bee in the photo to the right who took up residence in my sunflower patch last summer. This little one would tuck itself in between the petals at sunset and begin its day with a grooming session as the sun rose and the temperatures warmed up. It would move from bloom to bloom as the sunflowers faded and lost their petals – make sure you seed in succession for continued blooms from August through to late September.

Hummingbirds: It’s not just honey bees and natives that will visit your garden, you’ll see hummingbirds as well!
```python
# Import necessary libraries

# Fit the vectorizer to the training data
```

Sub Send_Email()
Dim olApp As Object
Dim olMail As Object
Dim EmailAddress As String

Set olApp = CreateObject("Outlook.Application")
Set olMail = olApp.CreateItem(0)

EmailAddress = ActiveCell.Value

With olMail
.To = EmailAddress
.Subject = "Email subject line"
.Body = "Email body text"
.Send
End With

Set olMail = Nothing
Set olApp = Nothing
End Sub

Explain quantum computing in simple terms

Quantum computing is a developing field of computing technology that utilizes the principles of quantum mechanics to process data. It is designed to leverage unique properties of quantum mechanics, such as superposition and entanglement, to potentially perform certain calculations more efficiently than classical computers.

In classical computing, information is stored and processed using bits, which can be either a 0 or a 1. Quantum computing, on the other hand, uses quantum bits, or qubits. A qubit can represent a 0, a 1, or both simultaneously due to superposition. This allows quantum computers to perform multiple calculations at once, unlike classical computers, which handle one calculation at a time.

Entanglement is another key feature of quantum computing, where qubits can be interconnected such that the state of one qubit can influence the state of another, regardless of the distance between them. This property may enable quantum computers to execute certain calculations more rapidly than classical computers, which are constrained by the speed of light.

Quantum computers are still in the early stages of development and are not yet widely accessible. However, proponents suggest they could eventually solve specific problems that are currently too complex or time-consuming for classical computers, such as breaking certain encryption methods or simulating intricate chemical reactions. Critics, however, note that significant technical challenges remain before these potential advantages can be fully realized.

As a CEO, you recognize the significance of fostering strong relationships with employees, partners, and customers. Trust and belief are two concepts that are often discussed in this context, each playing a distinct role.

While "trust" and "believe" are sometimes used interchangeably, they have different meanings. Trust involves a feeling of confidence in someone or something. When you trust someone, you have confidence that they will act in your best interest, fulfill their commitments, and be honest. Trust is typically developed over time through consistent experiences of reliability and dependability.

Belief, in contrast, involves accepting an idea or principle as true, which may or may not be based on evidence. Individuals may hold beliefs in certain principles, ideologies, or religious doctrines, even without direct evidence or experience.

In a business setting, trust is often seen as essential for building strong partnerships, as it facilitates effective collaboration and the achievement of shared goals. Belief can be viewed as a catalyst for innovation and progress, as it encourages confidence in one's own ideas and the potential for new opportunities.

In summary, trust is about confidence in someone or something, while belief is about accepting an idea or principle as true. Both trust and belief are important in building and maintaining relationships, but they serve different functions.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import re
import nltk

from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize
from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score
from tqdm import tqdm

# Set seed value
np.random.seed(42)

# Load data
train_df = pd.read_csv('train.csv')
test_df = pd.read_csv('test.csv')

# Compute class weights
class_weights = compute_class_weight(class_weight='balanced', classes=np.unique(train_df['label']), y=train_df['label'])

# Define text pre-processing functions
def preprocess_text(text):
    # Remove non-alphabetic characters
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z\s]', '', text)
    # Convert to lowercase
    text = text.lower()
    # Tokenize
    tokens = word_tokenize(text)
    # Remove stopwords
    tokens = [token for token in tokens if token not in stopwords.words('english')]
    # Lemmatize
    lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()
    tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(token) for token in tokens]
    # Join tokens back into a string
    text = ' '.join(tokens)
    return text

# Preprocess train and test text data
train_df['text'] = train_df['text'].apply(preprocess_text)
test_df['text'] = test_df['text'].apply(preprocess_text)

# Define KFold cross-validation
kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

# Define TF-IDF vectorizer
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer()

# Initialize F1 scores
f1_scores = []

# Train and evaluate model for each fold
for fold, (train_index, val_index) in enumerate(kf.split(train_df)):
    # Get train and validation data
    X_train, y_train = train_df.iloc[train_index]['text'], train_df.iloc[train_index]['label']

    # Compute TF-IDF features

    X_val_tfidf = tfidf.transform(X_val)

    # Train SVM model with class weights
    svm = SVC(class_weight={i: w for i, w in enumerate(class_weights)}, kernel='linear', random_state=42)
    svm.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)

    # Evaluate on validation set
    y_val_pred = svm.predict(X_val_tfidf)
    f1 = f1_score(y_val, y_val_pred, average='weighted')
    f1_scores.append(f1)
    print(f'Fold {fold+1} F1 score: {f1:.4f}')

    # Save predictions on test set for this fold
    X_test_tfidf = tfidf.transform(test_df['text'])
    y_test_pred = svm.predict(X_test_tfidf)
    test_df[f'fold{fold+1}'] = y_test_pred

# Compute average F1 score

# Ensemble predictions from all folds
test_df['label'] = test_df[[f'fold{fold+1}' for fold in range(5)]].mode(axis=1)[0]
```

C Language Overview
===================

C is a high-level, general-purpose programming language developed by Dennis Ritchie in the early 1970s. It was designed with portability, efficiency, and ease of use for systems programming in mind.

C is a compiled language, meaning it requires translation into machine code before execution by a computer. This translation process involves several phases that occur before the code is compiled and linked into an executable file.

The Four Phases of C Language
=============================

The four phases of the C language are:

1. Preprocessing Phase
----------------------

In this phase, the preprocessor reads the source code and performs tasks such as:

* Removing comments from the code
* Expanding macro definitions
* Including header files

The preprocessor produces a modified version of the source code, which is then passed to the next phase.

2. Compilation Phase
--------------------

During this phase, the modified source code is processed by the compiler, which translates it into assembly code. The compiler performs tasks such as:

* Checking the syntax of the code for errors
* Generating intermediate code
* Optimizing the code for efficiency

The compiler's output is a file containing assembly code.

3. Assembly Phase
-----------------

In this phase, the assembler takes the assembly code generated by the compiler and translates it into machine code. The assembler performs tasks such as:

* Converting assembly instructions into machine code
* Assigning memory addresses to instructions and data

The assembler's output is an object file containing machine code.

4. Linking Phase
----------------

In the final phase, the linker takes the object files generated by the assembler and links them to create an executable file. The linker performs tasks such as:

* Resolving external references
* Assigning memory addresses to object files
* Creating the final executable file

The linker's output is an executable file that can be run on the target machine.

Conclusion

How to improve instance segmentation AP metrics with human knowledge

Instance segmentation is a computer vision task that involves identifying and segmenting individual objects within an image. Improving instance segmentation AP (average precision) metrics can be approached by incorporating human annotation or labeling of the images.

Here are some ways human knowledge might be used to enhance instance segmentation AP metrics:

1. High-quality annotations: Supporters of human annotation argue that it provides high-quality ground truth data, which is essential for training and evaluating instance segmentation models. They believe that accurate annotations help ensure the model detects and segments objects correctly, potentially improving AP metrics.
2. Training data selection: Some experts suggest that human knowledge can aid in selecting training data that reflects the objects and scenes the model will encounter in real-world scenarios. This approach is thought to help the model handle various object types, lighting conditions, and other factors that may influence its performance.
3. Model interpretation: Human expertise can be utilized to interpret the output of the instance segmentation model, identifying errors or areas for improvement. This process may involve manually reviewing images to find instances where the model did not detect or segment objects accurately.
4. Model refinement: Human knowledge can contribute to refining the instance segmentation model by fine-tuning it for specific object types or scenarios. This might include adjusting model parameters, modifying training data, or using transfer learning to benefit from pre-trained models.

Overall, some believe that human knowledge can be a valuable resource for enhancing instance segmentation AP metrics by providing high-quality annotations, guiding data selection, interpreting model output, and refining the model itself. However, others may argue for alternative methods, and readers are encouraged to consider various approaches.
Can we apply human knowledge as a signal to improve instance segmentation in inference process

Yes, human knowledge can be applied as a signal to potentially enhance instance segmentation during the inference process. One approach involves post-processing techniques that integrate human insights into the segmentation outcomes.

This could involve manually correcting segmentation errors or employing automated algorithms that incorporate prior knowledge about object shapes and sizes. Another method to incorporate human knowledge into the inference process is through interactive segmentation. This approach allows users to interact with the segmentation results and provide feedback to the model. Additionally, human knowledge can be applied to post-process the output of the instance segmentation model to enhance downstream applications. How can I use conditional probability to improve instance segmentation in inference phase

Conditional probability can be applied to enhance instance segmentation during the inference phase by modeling the probability distribution of objects in an image based on the observed evidence. This approach can refine segmentation results by considering the relationships between objects and their context.

One method involves using conditional random fields (CRFs), a type of graphical model that can represent the joint probability distribution of objects in an image, conditioned on observed evidence. In instance segmentation, CRFs can model relationships such as spatial arrangements, object appearances, and the likelihood of certain object classes given the evidence.

Incorporating CRFs into instance segmentation involves using initial segmentation results as input to the CRF, which can refine these results by considering object relationships. For instance, CRFs can enforce spatial consistency, ensuring smooth and continuous object boundaries, and account for object appearances and class likelihoods based on observed evidence.

Another approach is through Bayesian methods, which model the posterior probability distribution of objects given observed evidence and prior knowledge. This can refine segmentation by integrating prior knowledge about objects, such as expected shapes or appearances.

In Bayesian methods for instance segmentation, prior distributions for each object class can be defined and updated based on observed evidence. The posterior probability distribution for each class is then computed using Bayes' theorem, considering both prior distributions and the likelihood of observed evidence.

Overall, conditional probability offers a means to improve instance segmentation during inference by considering object relationships and context. Techniques like CRFs and Bayesian methods can model these relationships and refine segmentation results, potentially leading to more accurate and robust outcomes.

```python
from detectron2.engine import DefaultPredictor
from detectron2.data import MetadataCatalog
from pydensecrf import densecrf
from pydensecrf.utils import unary_from_labels, create_pairwise_bilateral, create_pairwise_gaussian

# Load detectron2 configuration and model
cfg = get_cfg()
cfg.merge_from_file("path/to/config.yaml")
cfg.MODEL.WEIGHTS = "path/to/model.pth"
predictor = DefaultPredictor(cfg)

# Load image
image = cv2.imread("path/to/image.jpg")

# Run detectron2 instance segmentation
outputs = predictor(image)

# Extract class probabilities and predicted labels from detectron2 output
class_probabilities = outputs['instances'].scores.detach().cpu().numpy()
predicted_labels = outputs['instances'].pred_classes.detach().cpu().numpy()

# Initialize CRF
d = densecrf.DenseCRF2D(image.shape[1], image.shape[0], len(MetadataCatalog.get(cfg.DATASETS.TRAIN[0]).thing_classes))

# Add unary potentials (i.e., class probabilities) to CRF
U = unary_from_labels(predicted_labels, len(MetadataCatalog.get(cfg.DATASETS.TRAIN[0]).thing_classes), gt_prob=0.7, zero_unsure=False)
d.setUnaryEnergy(U)

# Add pairwise potentials to CRF
feats = create_pairwise_gaussian(sdims=(10, 10), shape=image.shape[:2])
d.addPairwiseEnergy(feats, compat=3)
feats = create_pairwise_bilateral(sdims=(50, 50), schan=(20, 20, 20), img=image, chdim=2)
d.addPairwiseEnergy(feats, compat=10)

# Run inference on CRF
Q = d.inference(5)

# Get refined segmentation mask from CRF
refined_labels = np.argmax(Q, axis=0).reshape(image.shape[:2])

# Display original image and refined segmentation mask
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 10))
axs[0].imshow(cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))
axs[0].set_title("Original Image")
axs[1].imshow(refined_labels)
axs[1].set_title("Refined Segmentation Mask")
plt.show()
```

(CNN)A sugar replacement called erythritol -- used to add bulk or sweeten stevia, monkfruit and keto reduced-sugar products -- has been linked to blood clotting, stroke, heart attack and death, according to a new study.

"The degree of risk was not modest," said lead study author Dr. Stanley Hazen, director of the Center for Cardiovascular Diagnostics and Prevention at the Cleveland Clinic Lerner Research Institute.
People with existing risk factors for heart disease, such as diabetes, were twice as likely to experience a heart attack or stroke if they had the highest levels of erythritol in their blood, according to the study, published Monday in the journal Nature Medicine.
"If your blood level of erythritol was in the top 25% compared to the bottom 25%, there was about a two-fold higher risk for heart attack and stroke. It's on par with the strongest of cardiac risk factors, like diabetes," Hazen said.
Additional lab and animal research presented in the paper revealed that erythritol appeared to be causing blood platelets to clot more readily. Clots can break off and travel to the heart, triggering a heart attack, or to the brain, triggering a stroke.
"This certainly sounds an alarm," said Dr. Andrew Freeman, director of cardiovascular prevention and wellness at National Jewish Health, a hospital in Denver, who was not involved in the research.
"There appears to be a clotting risk from using erythritol," Freeman said. "Obviously, more research is needed, but in an abundance of caution, it might make sense to limit erythritol in your diet for now."

ADVERTISEMENT
In response to the study, the Calorie Control Council, an industry association, told CNN that "the results of this study are contrary to decades of scientific research showing reduced-calorie sweeteners like erythritol are safe, as evidenced by global regulatory permissions for their use in foods and beverages," said Robert Rankin, the council's executive director, in an email.
The results "should not be extrapolated to the general population, as the participants in the intervention were already at increased risk for cardiovascular events," Rankin said.
The European Association of Polyol Producers declined to comment, saying it had not reviewed the study.
What is erythritol?
Like sorbitol and xylitol, erythritol is a sugar alcohol, a carb found naturally in many fruits and vegetables. It has about 70% of the sweetness of sugar and is considered zero-calorie, according to experts.
Artificially manufactured in massive quantities, erythritol has no lingering aftertaste, doesn't spike blood sugar and has less of a laxative effect than some other sugar alcohols.
"Erythritol looks like sugar, it tastes like sugar, and you can bake with it," said Hazen, who also directs the Cleveland Clinic's Center for Microbiome and Human Health.
"It's become the sweetheart of the food industry, an extremely popular additive to keto and other low-carb products and foods marketed to people with diabetes," he added. "Some of the diabetes-labeled foods we looked at had more erythritol than any other item by weight."
Erythritol is also the largest ingredient by weight in many "natural" stevia and monkfruit products, Hazen said. Because stevia and monkfruit are about 200 to 400 times sweeter than sugar, just a small amount is needed in any product. The bulk of the product is erythritol, which adds the sugar-like crystalline appearance and texture consumers expect.
An unexpected discovery
The discovery of the connection between erythritol and cardiovascular issues was purely accidental, Hazen said: "We never expected this. We weren't even looking for it."
Hazen's research had a simple goal: find unknown chemicals or compounds in a person's blood that might predict their risk for a heart attack, stroke or death in the next three years. To do so, the team began analyzing 1,157 blood samples in people at risk for heart disease collected between 2004 and 2011.
"We found this substance that seemed to play a big role, but we didn't know what it was," Hazen said. "Then we discovered it was erythritol, a sweetener."
The human body naturally creates erythritol but in very low amounts that would not account for the levels they measured, he said.
To confirm the findings, Hazen's team tested another batch of blood samples from over 2,100 people in the United States and an additional 833 samples gathered by colleagues in Europe through 2018. About three-quarters of the participants in all three populations had coronary disease or high blood pressure, and about a fifth had diabetes, Hazen said. Over half were male and in their 60s and 70s.
In all three populations, researchers found that higher levels of erythritol were connected to a greater risk of heart attack, stroke or death within three years.
But why? To find out, researchers did further animal and lab tests and discovered that erythritol was "provoking enhanced thrombosis," or clotting in the blood, Hazen said.
Clotting is necessary in the human body, or we would bleed to death from cuts and injuries. The same process is constantly happening internally, as well.
"Our blood vessels are always under pressure, and we spring leaks, and blood platelets are constantly plugging these holes all the time," Hazen said.
However, the size of the clot made by platelets depends on the size of the trigger that stimulates the cells, he explained. For example, if the trigger is only 10%, then you only get 10% of a clot.
"But what we're seeing with erythritol is the platelets become super responsive: A mere 10% stimulant produces 90% to 100% of a clot formation," Hazen said.
"For people who are at risk for clotting, heart attack and stroke -- like people with existing cardiac disease or people with diabetes -- I think that there's sufficient data here to say stay away from erythritol until more studies are done," Hazen said.
Oliver Jones, a professor of chemistry at RMIT University in Victoria, Australia, noted that the study had revealed only a correlation, not causation.
"As the authors themselves note, they found an association between erythritol and clotting risk, not definitive proof such a link exists," Jones, who was not involved in the research, said in a statement.
"Any possible (and, as yet unproven) risks of excess erythritol would also need to be balanced against the very real health risks of excess glucose consumption," Jones said.
Healthy volunteers
In a final part of the study, eight healthy volunteers drank a beverage that contained 30 grams of erythritol, the amount many people in the US consume, Hazen said, according to the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, which examines American nutrition each year.
Blood tests over the next three days tracked erythritol levels and clotting risk.
"Thirty grams was enough to make blood levels of erythritol go up a thousandfold," Hazen said. "It remained elevated above the threshold necessary to trigger and heighten clotting risk for the following two to three days."
Just how much is 30 grams of erythritol? The equivalent of eating a pint of keto ice cream, Hazen said.
"If you look at nutrition labels on many keto ice creams, you'll see 'reducing sugar' or 'sugar alcohol,' which are terms for erythritol. You'll find a typical pint has somewhere between 26 and 45 grams in it," he said.
"My co-author and I have been going to grocery stores and looking at labels," Hazen said. "He found a 'confectionery' marketed to people with diabetes that had about 75 grams of erythritol."
There is no firm "accepted daily intake," or ADI, set by the European Food Safety Authority or the US Food and Drug Administration, which considers erythritol generally recognized as safe (GRAS).
"Science needs to take a deeper dive into erythritol and in a hurry, because this substance is widely available right now. If it's harmful, we should know about it," National Jewish Health's Freeman said.
Hazen agreed: "I normally don't get up on a pedestal and sound the alarm," he said. "But this is something that I think we need to be looking at carefully."

The article from CNN presents a study that examines the potential link between erythritol, a widely used zero-calorie sweetener, and an increased risk of heart attack and stroke. What about cards for GMs? How can I make a system of encounter cards to help the GM tell a story and move the players through the narrative?

Encounter cards can be a useful tool for Game Masters (GMs) to manage the pacing of a game and create engaging experiences for players. Here are some balanced suggestions on how to design encounter cards for GMs:

1. Encounters: These can include events, challenges, obstacles, or characters that players interact with. Some GMs prefer to randomize encounters, while others tailor them to fit the narrative.
2. Types: Encounter cards can be categorized into various types, such as combat, social, exploration, or environmental encounters, allowing for diverse gameplay experiences.
3. Mechanics: Encounters may involve different mechanics, such as skill checks, card draws, dice rolls, or combinations thereof. These mechanics help determine the outcome and impact on players.
4. Points: Assigning a point value to encounters can indicate their difficulty or reward level. This can assist GMs in balancing encounters and providing a sense of progression.
5. Artwork: Including artwork on encounter cards can help set the scene and atmosphere. This artwork can be original or sourced from existing materials.

Using encounter cards, GMs can introduce unpredictability and excitement, while also having a tool to guide the game's flow. Encounters can be pre-made or created spontaneously, depending on the game's needs and the GM's preferences.

With the three pillars of gameplay being Combat, Exploration, and Diplomacy (or Social), encounter cards can be designed to align with one of these categories. Here are some ideas:

1. Combat: Combat encounters might involve battles with monsters, rival factions, or other challenges that require physical or magical abilities. These encounters could use mechanics such as dice rolls, card draws, or a combination of both to determine the outcome.
2. Exploration: Exploration encounters might include searching for treasure, discovering new locations, or solving puzzles. These encounters could use mechanics such as skill checks, card draws, or a combination of both to determine the outcome.
3. Diplomacy: Diplomacy encounters might involve negotiating with non-player characters, forming alliances, or resolving conflicts through conversation. These encounters could use mechanics such as skill checks, card draws, or a combination of both to determine the outcome.

By categorizing the encounters into one of these three pillars, the GM can tailor the encounters to fit the story and create a balanced and engaging experience for the players. Additionally, the GM can use the encounter cards to manage the pacing and flow of the game, ensuring that each pillar is represented and providing players with a variety of challenges to overcome.
How do I determine what skills can be used during which pillar of gameplay or type of encounter?

The skills applicable during each pillar of gameplay or type of encounter can be identified based on the specific nature of the encounter and the character type being played. Here are some perspectives:

1. Combat: Supporters of traditional role-playing games often highlight skills such as strength, agility, endurance, and weapon proficiency as commonly used in combat. Additionally, some players emphasize the importance of magical skills like spellcasting or elemental control in combat scenarios.
2. Exploration: In exploration, skills such as perception, survival, and thievery are frequently mentioned. Some players also value knowledge skills like geography or history for exploration encounters.
3. Diplomacy: In diplomatic situations, skills such as charisma, bluff, and negotiation are often cited. Additionally, knowledge skills such as etiquette or cultural awareness are considered useful by many players in diplomacy encounters.

When designing a skill system, it is generally advised to consider how skills will be utilized in each type of encounter, ensuring they are balanced and appropriate for the gameplay being represented. It is also suggested that players have a diverse set of skills to address a wide range of encounters, allowing them to apply their skills in various situations.
Instead of having a skill list, I’d like skills to be their own cards, with a wide variety of skills available. How can I make every skill usable in all the pillars of gameplay?

1. Multiple uses: Skills can be crafted to serve different purposes in various gameplay pillars. For instance, a "Deception" skill card might be employed in combat to feint and confuse an opponent, in exploration to mislead a guard or trick a trap, and in diplomacy to manipulate a non-player character. This approach is supported by those who value flexibility in gameplay.

2. Modifiers: Skills can be enhanced by other cards to alter their use. For example, a "Stealth" skill card could be used independently in exploration to avoid danger, but when paired with a "Sneak Attack" card, it could be utilized in combat to surprise an opponent. This method is favored by players who enjoy strategic combinations.

3. Contextual uses: Skills can be designed with contextual applications, making them more effective in specific gameplay pillars. For example, an "Intimidation" skill card might be used in combat to scare an opponent, in diplomacy to force a concession, and in exploration to bluff past a guard. This approach is appreciated by those who enjoy situational adaptability.

4. Versatile skills: Skills can be inherently versatile, allowing for use in multiple gameplay pillars. For instance, an "Insight" skill card could be used in combat to detect an opponent's weakness, in exploration to uncover hidden treasures, and in diplomacy to assess a character's motives. This versatility is valued by players who seek broad applicability.

By designing skills with versatility and multiple applications, players can engage with the game in diverse ways, enhancing the dynamic and engaging nature of the experience.

10. Choose the policy you modified or created from the "Calling policy" dropdown menu.
